utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, please continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. I hope you're fine.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else now. When my learned colleague, your counsel, Mr. Bakrac asked you some questions, you explained that you moved, that the command post moved several times during the war. Now, I first want to find out where the Pristina Corps command post was in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peacetime location of the corps command post was in the town of Pristina, in the headquarters building. This was a military building. It is in downtown Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you there during the war or did you abandon that position, and why?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite precise. When the state of war was declared, some of the forces had already gone and manned the wartime command post outside of Pristina. Some of the command organs remained for a couple of days in that old building, until the MUP building was hit, until some parts of the corps headquarters building were also damaged. And after that time, nobody came back to that building until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question -- and I have to apologise if my questions seem naive to you. I got as far as private first class in the army. So I want to know: What was the command post look like? Does the commander have to be there, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post is a set of people. It's not the most fortunate word, but it's a set of people, equipment, and the area, the surface area that has to be at least 4 to 6 square kilometres. It's a set of buildings, shelters, tents, the communications centre, the courier station. It's a -- it's a compound, a conglomerate of people, telecommunications equipment, equipment, buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During the war, as you said, you moved several times. There is evidence about that. You showed us Laus, and so on. At one point you told us that the Third Army commander was with you at all times. Was he there at that command post too and what did it look like? Where was the 3rd Army command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically, in physical terms, the army forward command post was part or, as we say, at the Pristina Corps command post. This means that the army commander was also there, because he was the leader of the forward command post of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When I see in your order that the Pristina Corps command post would be in the village of Laus, does that mean that at that time you and General Pavkovic were both there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may mean that, but not necessarily. It depends on the type of action. Such-and-such an action could be run by just a part of the corps command. It is -- it may not be necessary for the corps commander to run it, and least of all the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the command post. Is it necessary for you to be there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I believe that now we clarified the issue of what a command post is and now we can move on to something else. Yes. How does the command process go? What does it look like? You get something from the 3rd Army. I don't know. Whatever the chain of command is. And now the Pristina Corps should use part of its forces, half of its forces, the entire corps. What does it look like?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command process is a process in organisational, temporal, and technical terms. There are certain procedural functions, planning, organisation, ordering the execution of tasks, control, coordination, reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm interrupting, but I need you to explain how it functioned in wartime.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. The command system always has those procedural functions. I'm talking now about the wartime period. When a decision is received from the 3rd Army command, the corps command sets up a team -- sets up a team, because the corps command was not all in the same location -- a team that would study this task, prepare my basic concept, present the concept to the army commander, if he accepts it. Then the planning process starts. Planning takes several hours. After the planning is completed, the army commander verifies it on one of the documents. That's the decision map. And after that, the organisation process starts. Those documents are sent out to the subordinate commands or the subordinate commands, commanders, are summoned to a certain location to carry out preparations. They are handed the documents. The preparation is carried out. And two-thirds of the time allotted is then left to them for their own organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to put something to you and to get your opinion. In Prosecution exhibits we have 16 orders that are all entitled "Joint Command for KiM" and they are all unsigned. And it says "the Joint Command." Yes, yes the Joint Command. When the Defence and the Judges asked you, you explained why it was. And you said that was in the first 22 or 23 days of the war, until the 16th of April. And you explained who drafted all that, that this was drafted tat Pristina Corps, that it has all been logged in the logbook. I want to put it to you -- well, I will not be calling any of that up on the ELMO or in e-court, because everything is the same in all of those orders and we can all verify that. In all 16 -- or rather, not all of them were executed, but all of them contained in item 11, it says "Command and Communications." That is the heading. And there is a single sentence there, the first sentence that is repeated in all 16 orders, and it reads as follows: "The command post of the Pristina Corps in the peacetime location building." General, you said that that building was abandoned at the beginning of the war, that there was nobody there. You explained to us what the command post looked -- looked like. Could you please comment now. Is this, what I just read out, possible at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that it says this. And my explanation is the following: None of the counter-insurgency actions carried out during the war were carried out as a large-scale action or operation, as is the term that we've been using even in this courtroom, that would require the corps commander in its entirety to command and that would involve the entire corps. These were all mini anti-insurgency actions with the participation of -- between 0.2 up to several per cents of the Pristina Corps forces. That was the support for MUP and the Pristina Corps provided support with its combat groups that were part of the brigades. Not even brigades but combat groups that were part of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is clear, but we are now at a stage where we are trying to prove whether this piece of paper was repeated 16 times. We can see that this was drafted by computer. Is that possible or is this absurd? Yesterday when I asked you how many of these people were at those meetings in 1998, you said that there were some 10 people. According to this paper, it would appear that these 10 people, these 10 joint commanders, were sitting there in an empty building of the Pristina Corps commanding an action. This is what I'm asking you: Is it possible to do that without the troops, without the couriers, without the communications or anything? Is it conceivable at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. The corps command post, the main command post - and there are at least three command posts - but the main command post has the strength, if you count all the elements, of between five and six hundred personnel. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please give me a yes-or-no answer. Was it possible in these 16 orders to have the people sit there at the peacetime location of the Pristina Corps command post, those people that I mentioned, four civilians, the MUP, and whoever, the dozen people that we talked about, to sit there at the Pristina Corps command? Could you please say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely not possible, and it has nothing to do with what is written there, that the command post was in Pristina. And, of course, there were no civilians there, and now you're talking about four civilians or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In every order in item 11 there is this heading "Command and communication." That means that in those actions that are mentioned here, some had been carried out, some had not. I can conclude that the command and communications were not at the Pristina Corps command post in the peace-time location building. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Fila, if you are moving on to something else, could you identify one of these orders, please, so that we could have it on the screen briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have all the -- all of the 16 orders here with me. I can hand them over to him too. But let me just read it out. Let's, for instance, P1967. If you look at item 11 -- no, no, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Well, it's the one that you had up on the screen all the while the Defence counsel was examining the witness. That's 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have it on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 11, first sentence, PrK. It's on page 2. Item 11. And that's repeated 16 times, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you explain that sentence? No, it's -- that's the wrong page. Go back to the page we were on. In English, certainly. That's fine. Can you explain that first sentence of paragraph -- it may be II, I think. It's the Roman numeral 2, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's item 11. You can see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this kind of document with -- under this heading, this kind of orders that I explained a couple of days ago, they are part of the coordination plan and they show the subordinate units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yeah. I just want you to explain that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's what I'm trying to explain. This sentence in itself says what it says, but it doesn't actually mean what is written here. For the subordinate commanders, this means that the corps command would be located in its wartime location, although it says "peacetime location" here. The commanders know where the communications had -- have been rerouted and they know or they ask around to learn where the command post is located, and the corps command does not control this action. This is why this sentence means nothing for the subordinate commanders. It does not affect them in any way in this given situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is it there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is written here because this is a -- a model. This is a protocol format which requires that in item 11 the corps command post should be identified, which means that the subordinate units are responsible to the corps. They report to the corps. When you indicate that the command post -- when you identify a certain -- the command post of a certain structure in item 11, that means that the units are subordinate to that structure. And a practical reason, an additional reason of a practical nature is this: Although communications were encrypted to a certain degree, it was very easy to intercept those telegrams and we were able to hear the military district commander here. He testified that he was not aware at all times where the command post was but the corps command knew where its command post was. So in order to protect the confidentiality of this information, this is what was put here. And it was also put here for purely formal reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that we shall be able to see other orders which don't mention the Joint Command but are routine, proper orders, where there is a misleading statement of the location of the command post to avoid interception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In every other combat document, including the key document for the defence of the country, the order for the defence of the corps commander indicates quite accurately all the command posts: The main command post, the forward command post, the logistics command post, and all the other command posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be almost hyper-technical, but we're talking about a sentence that talks about peacetime location in a document that is a peacetime document. It's the 22nd of March, before the war has started. Now, it may be that that sentence appears in -- after the war starts in other documents, but -- and this may not be the best example for the exercise we've been going through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Fila, could we have one of these documents, please, which was produced during the war just to confirm whether or not it has that sentence in it. There is one, I recollect, actually signed by Mr. Lazarevic. Perhaps if -- if you know the number of it, then it might be the best one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for my turn to come. P01917 is the document you have here. P0 -- or, rather, P1969. Yes. Yes, 1969. The 28th of March. Yes. And you've got the 14th of April, P1972. Do you need more? There is more, if necessary, but I don't think we need more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it again paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's always 11. It's always 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you find paragraph 11, please. Mr. Hannis, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he did talk about using the one that the witness has signed, which is P1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what date is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's also the 22nd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but it has something different about the location of the command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can deal with that in cross-examination. Now, paragraph 11 doesn't appear in English to have this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why don't you read this in Serbian -- or let's have a look at another one. Never mind. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an illegible line. There is one -- the first line is illegible. And so --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be read out in the Serbian. But let's have a look at another one. No problem whatsoever. Have a look at P1972. I think that this is legible. It's legible here. P1972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you very much. You can proceed now, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General, you said that these documents from peacetime that are headed "Joint Command" were automatically transferred to wartime and that they automatically became documents of the Pristina Corps. Was this order perhaps transferred automatically as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted that this is a question of formalism, or formality. In these documents, just like this document itself has been compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I'd like to show you yet another example that this is being repeated automatically from peacetime onwards. Item 13. Any one of these. Let's have a look at the one we've got right in front of us, for instance. General, there are two sentences. And 16 times this same sentence is repeated unchanged. Does same go for that? Could you read 13.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Coordinated action with MUP forces in relation to preparing and carrying out combat activities should be organised prior to and during the implementation of combat activities with all forces during the course of implementing combat activities, all forces are commanded and led by the Joint Command for the KiM from the region of Pristina."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And we established that this was an absurdity, that this takes place in the peacetime building. Do you not infer that if that was so then these ten people would be sitting in that building there and they would be commanding the MUP from Pristina? The MUP, the army, the Air Force, maybe even the Navy in some way, or is this just an automatic thing, as you've just explained?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is done automatically, in terms of corresponding with subordinate units. However, you see paragraph 13? I have to remind you that according to combat documents, it has to do with a coordination cooperation. This additional part as -- that refers to "command and control," this is a technical, terminological thing that meant that there was concerted action, concerted command in an anti-terrorist action where there is no subordination among the forces involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. I think that will do as far as I'm concerned. And now perhaps I can move on. These 16 decisions, 16 documents called "Joint Command for KiM," did this in any way disrupt the chain of command to the Pristina Corps, briefly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, over the past few days, along parallel lines, along with these documents we showed here that in the case of subordinate units or in the corps command that is not the case. There is the corps command for the subordinate units, and they report to the corps command and they act in accordance with decisions made by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. So that means that once an action is over, those carried out, that is, those referred to in the documents entitled "Joint Command" -- when these actions are over, does anyone - anyone - report to some Joint Command about this? And finally, did this Joint Command exist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever sent a report to a Joint Command, because a Joint Command quite simply did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to -- two minor points. You said to the Honourable Trial Chamber in response to Mr. Bakrac's questions that you sustained losses in the Army of Yugoslavia, unnecessary ones, the police and -- or rather, the MUP and the army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You cannot just nod. You have to say whether you remember.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there -- had there been, rather, a Joint Command of this nature? If there had been people who coordinated all of this, would there have been these - what do you call them? Losses. Or would they have been reduced, at least?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military point of view, including the subject matter that you are talking about now, I am sure that the use of both forces would have been more efficient had there been a coherent Joint Command that could have made decisions on all matters. However, allow me to be consistent in terms of my own understanding of things. These two components of the structure of defence, it is very, very hard, even if someone gave orders five times, because these are different systems. It is hard to run both systems from one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You explained that with the same argumentation in terms of why re-subordination was an impossible task.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Last but not least, General, this is the last thing that I'm going to ask you about. You said that during the war you had 552 battles. And we have this Joint Command referred to only ten times during the first 22 days of the war. How could you have waged war at all without having Sainovic issue orders to you, as the Prosecutor says? How would you -- how were you capable of doing that without that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I want to say with full precision the documents with this kind of heading pertain only to the initial period of the war when support and coordination were regulated between the military and the police. There are no other documents from the entire war period, and there were several thousand documents. There are no other documents entitled this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You managed to wage war nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for three months we carried out our assigned tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I could have said "dobro jutro" too. I know those two words.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning. [Interpretation] I know that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the combat reports of the Pristina Corps. It appears that those combat reports after April of 1999 or beginning in April of 1999 were sent both to 3rd Army and the Supreme Command Staff. That seems unusual to me. Do you know why that was done?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer as to who ordered and when to have reports of the Pristina Corps sent simultaneously to the 3rd Army, as the superior command, and to the Supreme Command Staff. Probably the army command ordered the corps command to do that. This is a matter of my own assessment, that the army was ordered to do that by the corps. You asked me why, though. It is my assessment that the point of this reporting was for the Supreme Command Staff to obtain as soon as possible reports from the field. Let me add one more thing. This is also the principle of reporting from the border. For instance, border battalions report to the corps command and at the same time to the 3rd Army. They have three army -- three lines, three chains in peacetime as well. The 3rd goes to the General Staff. So that is my assessment and that is my response. Why these reports went to the immediate superior command and to the 2nd superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that what your answer is, that sometimes this leap-frog reporting is required because it's important to get information as quickly as possible?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence of my answer is that to shorten the time for information flows. But nothing is being skipped. I reported to the command of the 3rd Army and this second report is being cc'd in a way, as we say in the army, to the other command. We -- I sent my reports to the 3rd Army command. The other one perhaps did not say "copies to," but that is what it means, that it is -- that a copy is being sent to the Supreme Command Staff along with the previous document and along with the answer that I already gave, that it is important for them to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this period of time, from the beginning of the war until the end of the war, did you ever receive any objection from the Supreme Command Staff regarding the Pristina Corps reports that they were not providing sufficient information, not detailed enough? Did you ever receive any kind of an objection or instruction in that regard?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I, as a corps commander, the corps command never received objections from anyone that reports were not substantive, that they were not in keeping with procedure. I can just remind the Honourable Trial Chamber that they had the opportunity of seeing reports of five or six pages or even more than that. I myself was often dissatisfied because I did not have reports as to what the casualties were in the corps, how many people got killed. However, this is not a technical matter. It's not that no one wanted to report about this, but people were unaware of the situation on the ground. So practically every other day we got extraordinary reports and then we sent these extraordinary reports, special reports for the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps combat report, as I understand it, was compiled from reports that the corps command received from your subordinate units. Was there any filtering going on in that process? Were -- were you not reporting up to the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command important matters like, for instance, crimes that were being committed that you were -- the information you were receiving from the lower units? Was that not being reported up?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically rule out any possibility of, at the level of the corps command or the operations centre or anywhere else, having any kind of filtering taking place, in terms of concealing crimes. I absolutely rule out that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to move on to a slightly different subject, although related. You know that at the very beginning of the war, as the NATO bombing started, beginning as early as the 24th and maybe even in -- in anticipation a day or two before, that many civilians were leaving Kosovo. Do you know if any tried to leave Kosovo through territory where VJ was defending the border, or were they leaving through the normal border crossings or trying to leave through those normal border crossings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the entire duration of the war, that is, as much as I can be precise at this moment there, was only one occasion when on the left flank, facing Macedonia, a small group tried to illegally cross the state border - that is, not in an official border crossing - but unfortunately, they ran into a minefield. Two were lightly injured and the CO took them in his own car to Gnjilane to provide them with medical assistance. That was in one of the reports, and I'm aware of that one incident. Otherwise, there were no illegal crossings or attempted illegal crossings outside the official border crossings. As far as I know, there were two towards Macedonia and two towards Albania. Of course, I am not counting the crossings into Montenegro or Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. There is a document that I want you to look at, and I have a couple of questions to ask you about it. It's 4D510. And in the English, we're at the bottom of page 1. It's paragraph 3.1, the second paragraph beginning with "On 23 March." And that's all contained, I believe, on page 1 of the B/C/S. And as soon as it gets blown up a little bit, you'll probably be able to read it. Do you see that second paragraph beginning with . "On 23 March in the afternoon, a large column of refugees from Kosovo and Metohija was observed moving from the direction of Presevo towards Miratovac village with the intention of illegally crossing the DG" -- I think that's the state border. "DG security organs in the sector of the Cakanovac border post closed the passage, and the column of vehicles returned to Miratovac village. At about 1900 hours, most of the column left Miratovac village and headed for Kresevo." Now, first of all, this appears to be a situation where they were not permitted to cross the border into -- well, actually, let's look -- now that you've seen that -- and you've had a chance to read it; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Now to look at a map. So let's see if we can get 4D471 up on the screen. Now, we're going to need to do some -- some zeroing in on this map. Try to enlarge that area where there -- just to the right of where it says "EM" down in the bottom right-hand corner. Let's see. Do we have it there? Yes, I think so. Yes. Right up close to the top right-hand corner, you'll see Presevo. And just under that you'll see Miratovac. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What the report says is they were coming from Presevo and trying to cross the border in the area there of Miratovac. Now, Presevo is in Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that border crossing there near Miratovac is a border crossing into Montenegro, is it not? In Macedonia. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. So apparently what happened at this situation was this group of refugees that had apparently come out of Kosovo into Serbia was not permitted by the FRY forces, the FRY authorities, to cross over into Macedonia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written in the document. And I know every square foot of this territory and I have a complete picture in my mind, having read the description of the incident. That group of people had been returned to the official border crossing called Cukarka, because the place where they wanted to cross would have made the crossing illegal. That's why they had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing I'm interested in about this is this occurred on the 23rd, the day before NATO started bombing. If you -- you may not know. You may not have any information at all. But if you do know, could you tell us why -- why these refugees had -- had left Kosovo before the bombing started and were trying to cross then from Serbia over into Macedonia before there was even any bombing.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer why this group left on the 23rd, but I can say quite reliably what happened on the -- or what's happening on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, in terms of movements of people. And perhaps it's best for me to say that at that time it was clear to all of us that it was a question of hour, not day, when the war would begin, and a large number of the families of the members of the Pristina Corps were even then leaving Kosovo, mainly to Serbia and Montenegro, fleeing the possibility, the very real possibility of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was it -- was it widely known throughout Kosovo prior to the bombing beginning on the 24th that the OSCE mission had left the country? Was that widely known throughout the country? Did everyone pretty much know that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody knew and the media reported it widely. MUP secured them. The army was on stand-by to help if there should be any problems. The whole world knew and the public at large in Kosovo was aware of it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if that was generally seen by the people in Kosovo? And if you don't know, just say you don't know. But do you know if it was generally seen by the people in Kosovo as a -- as basically a war warning, a precursor to war, that war was coming?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 1.000, perhaps 1200 members of the OSCE were leaving Kosovo and Metohija at one point with about 100 vehicles. That mission had been stationed on the Albanian side and on the Serbian side in privately-owned facilities, so it was a widely known fact that they were leaving and that it was only a question of time when the airstrikes would begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I now want to go to another matter. On Friday in your testimony you were shown several documents primarily from the Pristina Corps regarding the protection of civilians. I would just like you to look at one more of those. It's P1766. Now, this is a document from 19 April 1999, and it comes from the 3rd Army command, General Pavkovic, to -- I take it, to your Pristina Corps and other units, and it deals with the same subject matter. The -- the preamble says that it's issued with a view to protecting the civilian population and directing them to safer areas. And then paragraphs 5, 6, and 7 are quite specific about what's to be done in that regard. And I presume that -- that this order from General Pavkovic provided a basis for some of the orders that you issued at about that same time. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And even if we look at that order I wrote, it contains a reference to the order of the army command, and following that order I envisaged certain activities within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now to a -- another subject matter. I -- I started with you this morning talking a little bit about your combat reports and the -- the issue of reporting. You -- you talked yesterday about the -- the different organs and the responsibilities of those organs, and you told us that with regard to the issue of crimes, that the organs primarily responsible for dealing with that was the -- the military security, the military police, and the military prosecutor and courts. There has been some contention by various witnesses in this case that the -- the crimes that occurred in Kosovo during the early days of the war were not being properly reported up to chain of command. And I'm sure you've heard that evidence. And at least one point in the trial a suggestion or a question was asked regarding whether or not the military security organs did not have their own reporting chain through which they would be reporting these kinds of activities had they noticed. You will also recall both General Farkas and General Vasiljevic telling us that their inspections at the Pristina Corps indicated to them that all the crimes were being detected and prosecuted properly and that the only issue was an issue of failing to report properly up the chain of command. I think a lingering question about this whole area has to do with whether the security department, in fact, did have its own reporting chain. And in that connection, I'd like to show you two or three documents, just as exemplary documents. Look at first 5D1310, please. Now, this appears to be a document in the nature of a report that's from the security department -- the security department of the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command Staff in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was sent to the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like you to just sort of glance through the document, and I'll have the -- the pages paged through kind of one at a time, but I -- I don't want to spend a lot of time but I just want you to look at the nature of this document, see what kinds of things were contained in it. So let's go to the second page now. And tell me when you've kind of made your way through that page and then we'll go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, then, please. And finally the last page.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can move on. I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, do you agree with me that this appears to be not some unique report dealing with some unique situation but more in the nature of a regular -- a regular report? Reporting a number of different matters. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that at least six, seven, or eight security topics were covered: The situation around, the situation on the territory, treatment of the arrested members of the military department Prizren who were sent to the military court in Pristina after kidnapping by terrorists, application of various measures. Practically the activities of the 3rd Army over a couple of days. Mr. Walker is also mentioned and his activities in Macedonia with refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I want to look at paragraph 13, on the last page, because I think that's significant. And we were there and then we went back to the first page for some reason. But we'll go to the last page of the document again, please. One page back in English. Look at paragraph 13. Paragraph 13 reports about criminal activities of members of the VJ, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain First Class Dejan Radovanovic -- I dare say that I know, perhaps not so precisely at this moment, but I recognise the person by name, unless there are two of them with the same first and last names. So this man I know was from the Nis Corps of the 3rd Army, that is, outside Kosovo and Metohija. He was arrested. And from subsequent information, I know that he was working in the encryption service. He had been charged and indicted. And I believe this is a reference to that criminal act, from all I know. And the security administration is being informed of it. .

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The point is it's the -- it's the reporting up the chain of command of criminal activity that's being dealt with in the VJ, isn't it? You can just say "yes" or "no" to that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look now at 5D1311. And we can deal with this very quickly. This is another security department report to the Supreme Command Staff. And this one sends along a couple of witness statements taken from a couple of members of the KLA. Again, this is detailed information, not some, you know, specific non-regular kind of reporting process. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this is a special report, judging by the first item of the previous report. I know of this incident when two members of terrorist forces were arrested in the area of Gnjilane, where they admitted that they had killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... knowledge of that situation. I am only trying to establish that this kind of reporting was going on on a regular basis. And you -- you know that it was, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the report is self-explanatory. It indicates clearly from who -- from whom it comes, whom it was sent to, when.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, very quickly we'll look at one more. It's 3D1038. This one is slightly different. This one is from the Pristina Corps command security section. And not only does it go to the 3rd Army command, which one would expect, but it also goes straight up to the security administration of the General Staff and also to the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group. So this is another example of a security report from Pristina Corps or an example that is not going just to the 3rd Army but straight on up to the General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we have seen a number of similar documents even here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is in the nature, just looking at the headings in it, of a situation report, the reporting on the situation on the border and the situation in the territory. And, again, this looks like part of a regular reporting process. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this is a regular security report containing the standard items, the standard paragraphs that are permanent to this format.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, to avoid going through a number of more -- of similar documents, simply for the record I'll tell you that 5D1306, 5D1307, 3D1001, and 3D1035 are of the -- of similar nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the testimony of General Farkas, General, he was asked by me if he was aware that virtually every 3rd Army combat report during the wartime obtained a section reporting on crimes. And this is at transcript 16322 and 323. General Farkas told me that was impossible because if there had been such reporting, General Gajic would have informed him, and he never got that information from General Gajic. I want to know if you have seen any of the 3rd Army combat reports from that period of time containing that paragraph regarding the activities of the prosecutors and military courts. Have you seen those documents?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army from the forward command post were practically drafted in the same room, in the same building. I've seen a large number of them, without going into the substance, but they derived their contents from the reports of the Pristina Corps. And in this entire process, I have seen a large number of these reports. And I'm talking about the wartime in this first segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, rather than look at a number of these, I'm just going to again tell you that, just as an example, 4D307 from the 30th of March, 4D273 from the 31st of March, 4D274 from the 1st of April, 4D275 from the 2nd of April, 4D276 from the 3rd of April, 4D409 from the 5th of April, and it goes on and on almost daily through the entire war period that these reports have a paragraph reporting on crime activities in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Your Honours will recall yesterday - so I don't have to repeat it with the general today - his testimony that the regular reporting from his subordinate units didn't really get underway until around the 31st of March, when he started getting kind of regular reports that were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look now at another document. This is 4D420. This is a document from General Pavkovic to the Supreme Command Staff, personally to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, dated the 20th of April, 1999. And this relates to the action that had taken place at Rogovska Klisura, and I take it you were quite familiar with that action.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like you to look at the explanation of General Pavkovic there in paragraph 1 and just tell the Judges whether or not based upon your knowledge of that action his report is an accurate report.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preparations for this action cited as early as in the first half of March, in organisational terms, the orders were issued to establish coordination between the 3rd and the 2nd Army -- or rather, the 2nd Army and the Pristina Corps. Some documents were exchanged between the 3rd Army and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, as it was at the time. An order was also issued. That was headlined "The Joint Command." That's the famous order. But as far as I can recall, there were some problems regarding the implementation of this task within the given time, and I would go as far as to say that this action lasted until May and that we repeated orders, repeated activities, coordination, the organisation. As -- and as far as this segment that is described here, there are several reports from the Pristina Corps and probably from the 3rd Army command too that some of the elements from the 125th Motorised Brigade, a light infantry battalion, had set up the blockade and that from Montenegro the MUP forces were searching the terrain. But it lasted for a very, very long time. This action could not be completed within the time it was planned. It was a very complicated situation around Rogovska Klisura.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I could ask --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this was just the beginning of this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have to ask you the question again, though. My question -- let me -- let me ask it a little different. Are you -- have you seen this document before seeing it just now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it -- I've seen it recently at the trial here. Maybe some 10 or 15 days, whatever it was that it was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see it at the time of the action, around the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see this document, but I know what the agreements were. I know what the orders were, what the army command, what the army commander did, what I did together with my units in coordination with the Podgorica Corps and some MUP elements. I have this whole picture in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I could go back to my original question. Is the information contained there in paragraph 1 accurate?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't confirm, but there is no reason for me to doubt what it says here, that the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia issued this task. If the army commander says this, then it is probably true. But I was never in a position to meet with the President of Yugoslavia or even to see him in 1998 or in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to have to be more specific, because we're not getting ... I'm interested in the part of this paragraph that reads as follows: "In this operation, the following VJ units were engaged in the blockade of the general area of Rogovska Klisura and were not envisaged as taking active part. The 2nd Battalion of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade and the 1st and 2nd Corps Artillery Group of the Pristina Corps and some of the units of the 2nd Army." And I emphasise "not envisaged as taking active part." "This is why we could not halt the said operation, because it was planned and organised by the competent MUP command." Now, this is on the 20th of April, which is, I think, the day after that operation actually started. And you've explained that it went on for a very long time after that. Based upon what you know, is this an accurate explanation of that action up to that point?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that the units of the 2nd Light Infantry Battalion of the 58th Brigade were manning the blockade line in the hilly part of Rogovska Klisura and some of the MUP elements from Kosovo and Metohija were engaged in combat -- or rather, from Montenegro. I don't know who was engaged in combat from that area in the effort to route the terrorist forces. And then things would stop and then would continue up until the beginning of May. But in the initial period, this is the picture of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We're going to another matter now. I want you to look at 5D436. Now, what you see on the screen is a 27 May 1999 report to Colonel General Ljubisa Velickovic. And this report is authored by General Terzic regarding his inspection of the 354th pbr and other units. First of all, I'm sure you're familiar that General Velickovic came to Pristina with a group of people to conduct this tour of inspection in May of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go over to the paragraph right before paragraph 4 of the report, which is page 5 in English, and I don't know where in B/C/S but we'll find it. It's right before paragraph 4, which says "Conclusion." Next page. It's page 4, I think, in B/C/S. It would be the next page -- no, wait a minute. I think you may have it there. Yes. In English, we're on page 5. There we are. We got it. And it's paragraph 9 there that we're interested in. General Terzic -- the part that I'm mostly interested in: "There is no single command in the zone of responsibility of the brigade." And then there's some additional things about dissatisfaction with MUP and things of that nature contained in that, but the part I'm interested in is "no single command." And then if you go over to paragraph 5. It would be the next page. Number 1. He points out that: "All the problems observed fall within the competence of the command, the army, the corps, and the brigade. The Supreme Command Staff should provide assistance in securing communications equipment, establishing clearly outlined relations with the MUP organs and units, and taking measures to provide care for families of soldiers through the governments of FRY and Serbia." Okay?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now I want you to look at 5D434. Now, this document is dated the 2nd of June, 1999, a few days later. And this is a compilation by General Velickovic of all of the reports that he received during this inspection of the Pristina Corps. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we look over -- it's on page 4 in the English, paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for the record, this is the same document as 3D692 that had been used before during the trial. It will -- it will make it easier to follow things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll note the connection. But just continue using this one for the moment, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 11. General Velickovic basically repeats in many respect what is General Terzic had told him, and apparently it was a broader issue: "In the zone of responsibility, there is no unity of command all over forces. Relations with the MUP have been maintained through agreements which have frequently not been respected, particularly at lower levels. "Even though this cooperation is functioning for the time being, in serious crisis situations and when there is no time, it can have serious consequences both for Yugoslav Army soldiers and members of MUP." That's what he reports; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here. But if you need my comments, you can ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's totally consistent, General, isn't it, with what you have told the Trial Chamber about, the problem of non-subordination of MUP, and that is that it caused unnecessary deaths of both police and soldiers because of a lack of -- of complete coordination. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Trial Chamber's leave and by your leave, let me say that coordination and command are two different things. So there was no re-subordination. There is not a single subordination in chain of command. Relations are based on cooperation, coordinated action and coordination. That is not the same as command. You said that there was no coordination. Coordination was there at the level of cooperation, but there was no command relationship. This is something completely different. This team noted the problems and informed the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, as they did about the other problems, communications, soldiers who died due to blood loss because there had been no communications equipment in place, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to remind you -- I want to go to the next page under "Proposed measures." And you see that. It says that "The 3rd Army command -- the 3rd Army command should urgently analyse the outlined and other weaknesses and start removing them in a planned manner. And forward one copy of the plan to the Supreme Command Staff. Resolve all problems that the 3rd Army command cannot resolve within its competence via the Supreme Command Staff through regular requests." Now, that's what General Velickovic basically, if not ordered, suggested to General Pavkovic regarding this report. And I'd like you now to look at a document from General Pavkovic two days later, P1725. This is a 4 June 1999 document. If you look at the line that says "re" or "beza." Mr. Visnjic is going to tell us his number or something --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection to this comment by my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman, who said regarding the previous document that this was a document in which General Velickovic suggests to the 3rd Army commander what should be done. But the document that was shown to the witness, this is not a document that is addressed to the 3rd Army but to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. This document by General Velickovic is not sent to the 3rd Army commander but to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. So if any suggestions are made, there's -- they are made to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, not to the 3rd Army commander, as was put to this witness by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, that's -- that's really an interesting objection, because if you look at the 4 June document, the "re" line, General Pavkovic indicates that he is specifically addressing the 29 May 1999 document, number 03/5520-1, which is 4D434. So he definitely had it in his hands, it definitely was sent to him. And it definitely says in that document what it is he should do, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your respective comments are noted and will be evaluated in due course. Please proceed with the question you want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at paragraphs 1 and 2 of this document. In English it's on the second page. First of all, General Pavkovic says: "In order to ensure the necessary level of combat readiness in the Pristina Corps, we request that the following problems affecting the combat readiness of the Pristina Corps, which a Supreme Command Staff team noticed while visiting some of the units from 23 through 26 May 1999, be solved on the Supreme Command Staff level and through responsible organs of the Federal Ministry of Defence, the Federal Republican government," and so on. And then he sets out three things here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I'm looking at the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are, Your Honour. I was just -- I was reading from page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And showing page 2 here. Do you want to go back to page 1 and look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. No, no. Please ask your question. It's -- it's sounding rather like a submission, all of this, rather than a -- an examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 1, you'll see that General Pavkovic is basically speaking of the same issues, the MUP forces not being re-subordinated, something about privileged position of MUP members, and some other matters. This is basically a reflection, is it not, of what was contained in the Velickovic report?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And if you allow me, there is no dilemma here. I know that we discussed this often with the army commander, how to resolve this problem, but there were no orders from the Ministry of the Interior and throughout the war it was always coordination and no -- not re-subordination. And in this item 1, the army commander stresses this problem once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I know you're familiar with documents 4D192 and P1459. These are your report of the 24th of May and Pavkovic's nearly identical report of the 25th of May regarding the failure of subordination of -- of MUP. You're familiar with those documents, are you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's the case, isn't it, that you and General Pavkovic were reporting on the 24th and 25th of May basically the same problems that Generals Terzic and Velickovic were reporting on the 27th of May and the 2nd of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence is that the order for the re-subordination of the MUP forces had not been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to a different subject now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we possibly break then, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, I want you to look now at P1467. What you see is a 31 May warning issued by General Pavkovic, and it says "To the commander himself." I assume that means you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This seems to be a document of frustration on General Pavkovic's part that issues regarding the security of roads are simply not being dealt with properly. And you're obviously familiar with this order. If you look at -- it's page 2 in English. He says: "In order to control losses in manpower and TMS, I order the subordinate commands" -- then he uses the words "one last time" -- "to secure the passage of m/v" -- whatever that is -- "in their zones of responsibility and prevent ambushes," and so forth. I'm interested in your explanation of this, if you understand what he's talking about, and particularly that language "one last time." Can you explain this at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. I know what this is all about. In the central part of Kosovo and Metohija and along the main roads leading to Drenica, in late May mines were laid quite extensively. That was stepped up by the terrorist forces. And at the same time, acting in concert, there were attacks launched from Albania and huge losses were sustained throughout Kosovo and Metohija and full control of the territory had not been established, as had been ordered to us. We were supposed to do that together with the MUP forces through the system of re-subordination. And the army commander had ordered -- issued an order a week ago, I think to the MUP forces too, but on this occasion he simply issues an order to me to prevent at all costs and in concert with the MUP forces any losses. So this is the essence of the last order. But I think that there was another order that followed after this one, because this was a war. But the gist of it is that the army commander is demanding in quite energetic terms that the passabilty of roads and the prevention of losses should be ensured in coordination with the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's look now at another -- actually, we're going to look at a map. I take it you're familiar with the Ratis action in September 1998? And we'll look at the map 4D495. Now, I had asked you if you were familiar with this action. I don't know that you answered that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we need to look at the entire map, rather than zooming in. You've seen this map before.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see it at the time of the action in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. I'm not entirely sure, but I think so. I know that I was there in the field, and the purpose was -- of the action was to find the victims of the terrorist forces in this area, quite a number of them, in Radonjic Lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the last time this map came up, as you will recall in this Chamber, there was a question about why General Pavkovic's signature doesn't appear at the lower right-hand corner, like it ordinarily would. Do you have any explanation as to why it's not there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I see a map of this sort in front of me, I cannot claim with complete certainty that this is not a decision of the army commander and there -- there shouldn't be the signature of the Chief of Staff of the army. I don't know whether this is a decision from the Pristina Corps or from the 3rd Army commander. I know that he made the decision for this action, and that is why I cannot give you an answer why there is no signature from General Pavkovic, the corps commander. Perhaps the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, General Simic, was supposed to sign this or somebody else from the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you see a signature in the upper left-hand corner under the name "Dusan Samardzic"; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is approved by the 3rd Army commander. And if this is his decision and not the decision of the corps commander, then in the right-hand corner there should be a signature from someone from the army. And if this is a decision of the corps commander, then in the right-hand corner there should be the signature of the corps commander. But I cannot confirm whose map this is. In accordance with the rules on the working map, there should be a signature in the right-hand corner of the person who made this map and whose decision this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you generally about the activities of the VJ in 1998. As I understand it, there were basically two -- two kinds of activities. There were planned actions and then there were activities that would result in a kind of self-defence situation where a VJ unit would be fired on and respond. And I want to restrict my question to those actions that were planned, that were not self-defence actions but were planned actions. Do you know if in every case those planned actions were approved by General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Trial Chamber's leave, I would like to say that the initial decision for every action, including the smaller scale ones in which just one combat group from the Pristina Corps participated, was made by General Samardzic, the 3rd Army commander, or General Simic, the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, and only then did the Pristina Corps command make plans on the basis of this decision, but the plan had to be first verified by the 3rd Army commander. As far as I know, in 1998, while I was at the forward command post in Djakovica, throughout this period all activities were planned and approved by General Samardzic and the 3rd Army command, when we're talking about the use of the Pristina Corps forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Do you know if any action during --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if any action during 1998 carried out by forces of the Pristina Corps under orders from General Pavkovic that had not been approved by General Samardzic or General Simic, as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such action. And if I may be allowed to say something from a military standpoint, it is simply not possible to make such a decision without the approval of the superior. When we're talking about the use of the units in which lives of the soldiers may be lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, we're going to go to one final matter, and I'm going to use a document we saw earlier today. That's P1966. And I want to go back to paragraph 13 on the last page. The first sentence of paragraph 13 says this: "Organise coordinated action with MUP forces concerning preparations for combat operations before the start and during the combat operations." The question I have for you about that is: If what was going on here was a true joint operation under one single command, there wouldn't have been any necessity for this paragraph, would there? This paragraph is basically ordering some planning and cooperation. That wouldn't be necessary in a true joint operation; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. But if you allow me, this is a counter-terrorist action, not operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, the other question I want to ask you is about that last paragraph that we see over and over in these documents. It says: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command and direct all forces during combat operations ...." We've had trouble getting a -- I think a decent explanation for what that means, so I'm going to try again. When -- when an action like this was being carried out, when it was actually going on on the ground, there had to be some kind of a command post that was directing that action; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about the use of the army units, then definitely. And this order, as you can see, pertains to units of the army, the use of the elements of the Pristina Corps. And there must be either at the level of the brigade or combat groups or two or three brigades acting on separate axes the command element that would be in command of all those forces for their part of the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would have been a specific location with specific personnel there directing actions during the -- the -- that action, while it was going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we just looked at the map of Ratis, for instance, and we saw that it was both VJ units and MUP that were involved in that action. So would I be correct that in that command post as that action was going on, there were commanders for both VJ and MUP directing their respective forces? Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, but you're not always right. It does not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My wife would appreciate that last comment?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I previously spoke, I tried to explain that this sentence was extracted from some other terms, that combined command allowed for the possibility that at a given point in time the commander of the unit is in his position, the commander of the police unit is in his position. But at one point, in order to directly find a solution to some problems, they can both find themselves in a single place, either the commanders themselves or their liaison officers, and they can follow how some combat actions develop together. That is this combined activity. Every one of them commands their own forces. After a few hours, they all go to look at their own units. They part ways. So that is this combined command that somebody christened "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've spoken during your testimony about 1999 and the forward command post and how there was a very close cooperation between you and General Pavkovic, that you would see each other almost daily. I'm wondering if that -- that kind of an arrangement, a similar kind of an arrangement existed during 1998 when General Samardzic was 3rd Army commander and Pavkovic was Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the Honourable Trial Chamber, may I intervene at this point? I did not cooperate with the army commander. I was subordinated to him. His forward command post was at the command post of the corps. I carried out his orders. It can be accepted from a nonmilitary point of view that we had cooperation in terms of understanding war-related problems, but our relationship in the war was that General Pavkovic was at the command post of the Pristina Corps and in 1998 General Samardzic was practically at the command post of the Pristina Corps, where he had to, to the best of my understanding and knowledge,-- or rather, where the commander of the Pristina Corps had to report at least twice a day. The difference was that throughout the war we were carrying out our tasks. But I know that at least twice a day the corps commander had to report to the forward command post, to General Samardzic and his organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mistakingly used the word "cooperation" when I intended to use the word "coordination." I even wrote "coordination" here in my question. I think you understood it that way, and that's all the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. 44, line 9. "We were carrying out the task at the -- at the command post together," I believe the -- the witness says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic, I will -- I will deviate from my usual manner of identifying myself since you know who I am at this point in the proceedings. But I will caution you. I know it's been a long week and a half for you, but I would ask that you please try as much as possible to pay close attention to what I have to ask. And if one -- any one of my questions is not clear to you, please make it known to me so that I can re-ask the question. Otherwise, I will try to move through the topics that I have as efficiently as possible so as to minimise the amount of time that you have to stay on the stand. But we do have a lot of things we need to go through. Now, first of all, as a preliminary matter, while it is still fresh in everyone's mind and before I forget about it, the Trial Chamber -- when you testified during the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Fila, the Trial Chamber asked -- well, you indicated that the "zapovesti" that say the "Joint Command for KiM," when you said that those had the peacetime location of the Pristina Corps as their command centre for reasons to avoid intercepts revealing the true location, Judge Bonomy inquired and asked of you if that could be proven by showing a "zapovest" from -- that did not refer to the Joint Command but it also referred to this location where the Pristina Corps command was in fact not. If that makes sense for you, I'd like to first start off with Exhibit 6D704, which I believe is in fact exactly what Judge Bonomy was asking about and which I think shows and proves your position that in fact the use of the term - I don't know if I can find it - [B/C/S spoken] [Interpretation] In the -- [In English] Regularly for documents that are labeled as being Pristina Corps command, Zapovesti. " JUDGE BONOMY: Mr. Ivetic; just have a look at the transcript in front of you and see how much space and time you have occupied on going nowhere so far and let's try to be efficient by just getting to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will. I will. Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have a comment, maybe a request. I'm impressed with Mr. Ivetic's use of Serbian, but the problem is it creates a transcript that is largely unable to be followed, and I think it would be much more useful if he would use the English words so that we get a transcript that we can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we agree with that. The -- the points that you seek to make by being specific in this way, Mr. Ivetic, can be made in submissions, because we have access obviously to what's said in Serbian in the documents where you may seek to -- to draw a distinction because of a particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The use of particular language. But it probably is better to make the transcript consistent. And if you do feel the need to use the Serbian word specifically, then I think you should also use what is the English equivalent according to the current translation of it. That's the available translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe this one does not have a translation, which is why I had to use the Serbian word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because I did not -- this is actually an item that I did not plan to go into, but since it came up in Your Honour's question, I thought I would bring it to the Court's attention that there is a Zapovest -- there is a order that originates from the command of the Pristina Corps that does not anywhere in it mention the Joint Command or the Joint Command for KiM but which does, in fact, as the general has already indicated, have the information that the command will be conducted from the command building of the Pristina Corps in its peacetime location, which I believe is the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- just ask him to -- since we don't have a translation, just ask him to read the sentence in the document which is now before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic, if I can beg your indulgence. If I could have you look at the last page of this exhibit in e-court. And once it comes up, I will ask you to read item 11, which is the command and communications portion of this order from the Pristina Corps command, the first line which is similar to the lines which you've gone through with Mr. Fila. If you could just read that for us, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The command post of the Pristina Corps in the building of the peacetime location."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the date of that document, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 4th of May, 1999, as far as I've mentioned to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
